html:
Ghazni is a city in southeastern Afghanistan, on a high plateau on the road from Kabul to Kandahar. Around the year 1000 it was the capital of an empire that stretched from Iran into north India.

In earlier centuries it was a Buddhist centre in the land of Zabulistan, under the Zunbil kings. The Saffarids took it around 870. In the 960s a Turkic slave general seized the town, and his successor Sabuktigin founded the Ghaznavid dynasty there in 977.

Under Sabuktigin's son Mahmud, who reigned from 998 to 1030, Ghazni grew rich on plunder from raids into India, such as the sack of Somnath in 1025. Mahmud filled it with mosques, palaces and scholars. He brought al-Biruni there, who went on to write his book on India, and the poet Ferdowsi presented the Shahnameh to him.

In about 1150 the Ghurid ruler Ala al-Din Husayn burned the city for seven days, earning the name "World Burner". The Ghurids then made it a base for their own conquest of India. The Mongols destroyed it in 1221, and it never regained its old size. Two tall brick minarets of the Ghaznavid sultans still stand. The British stormed its fortress in 1839, in the First Anglo-Afghan War.
